must_remember: To convert a moving coil galvanometer into a voltmeter, a very high resistance called a multiplier ($R$) is connected in series with the galvanometer coil.
An ideal voltmeter possesses infinite internal resistance and draws zero current from the circuit under test.
Voltmeter sensitivity ($S$) is defined as the reciprocal of the full-scale deflection current ($I_g$), expressed in ohms per volt ($Omega/V$).
The series resistance required to extend the voltage range up to $V$ is given by $R = \frac{V}{I_g} - G = G(n - 1)$, where $n$ is the range multiplication factor.
A practical voltmeter causes a loading effect due to its finite internal resistance, leading to an apparent measured voltage lower than the true open-circuit voltage.

glossary.meaning: A very high resistance connected in series with a galvanometer to convert it into a voltmeter.
The reciprocal of the galvanometer full-scale deflection current, measured in $Omega/V$.
The disturbance caused in a circuit when a non-ideal voltmeter draws a minute fraction of current, altering the node voltages.
The ratio of the new maximum voltage range to the initial voltage range of the galvanometer ($n = \frac{V}{V_g}$).
